title: Trump Imposes 15% Tariff and Price Floors on Polysilicon to Counter China
excerpt: The White House invoked a Cold War-era trade law to shield U.S. polysilicon makers from Chinese competition, setting minimum import prices across the solar and semiconductor supply chain.
body:
• President Trump imposed a 15% tariff and minimum import prices on polysilicon and derivative products under Section 232, effective December 4.
  • The action targets Chinese dominance in a material critical to both solar panels and semiconductors, with China controlling roughly 80% of global solar manufacturing capacity.
  • U.S. solar stocks rallied sharply on the news, with Corning up 9.4%, T1 Energy up 9.9%, and First Solar gaining 4.7%.
  • Industry groups warn the tariffs could raise costs for solar projects and consumer electronics, even as some manufacturers welcome the protection.

The White House on Thursday imposed a 15% tariff and a series of price floors on polysilicon and its derivative products, invoking the Cold War-era Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 to protect domestic producers from Chinese competition in a material that underpins both the semiconductor and solar industries.

The proclamation sets minimum import prices of $21 per kilogram for polysilicon, $100 per kilogram for ingots and wafers, $0.22 per watt for solar cells, and $0.38 per watt for solar modules. The protections take effect on December 4, according to the White House.

A Strategic Material at the Center of Two Industries

Polysilicon, an ultra-pure form of silicon, sits at the start of both the semiconductor and solar manufacturing supply chains. The chip industry accounts for just 2.4% of global polysilicon demand, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association, but domestic semiconductor manufacturing — a stated Trump priority — depends on the solar industry's larger demand to keep U.S. polysilicon production economically viable.

"They're finding that they actually do need solar," said Rhone Resch, chief strategy officer at Japan's Toyo Co Ltd, which operates a solar panel factory near Houston and plans to invest $357 million in a nearby solar cell facility.

The trade action aims to protect U.S. polysilicon factories owned by Hemlock Semiconductor, a joint venture between Corning and Japan's Shin-Etsu Handotai, and Munich-based Wacker Chemie, which runs a plant in Tennessee.

"Without polysilicon, the next steps of the value chain — wafer and chips or wafer and solar cells — are not possible."

— Wacker Chemie, in a statement

Markets React, but Concerns Linger

Solar and semiconductor-adjacent stocks rallied on the news. Corning closed up 9.4%, T1 Energy climbed 9.9%, First Solar gained 4.7%, and Canadian Solar advanced 5.6%, according to Reuters.

But the administration faces a delicate balancing act. Industry groups representing solar developers and semiconductor buyers have warned that the tariffs could raise costs for solar power plants and increase prices for consumer electronics and automobiles at a time of surging demand from the AI data center boom.

"The market might start having projects fall down" if costs become too high, said Martin Pochtaruk, CEO of panel maker Heliene, which operates factories in Minnesota. He called the solar industry's role in the chip-focused investigation "collateral damage."

The Broader Trade Picture

The polysilicon action is part of a broader Trump administration push to rebuild U.S. manufacturing through tariffs. The president has already completed Section 232 probes and imposed tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum, copper, and lumber, with investigations into drones, industrial robots, pharmaceuticals, and critical minerals still underway.

The Commerce Department plan includes provisions allowing importers investing in U.S. wafer and cell production to offset tariff costs, as well as an incentive program for companies building domestic polysilicon factories.

Some in the industry had lobbied for a faster 90-day implementation timeline, arguing the 120-day window gives China too much time to sell into the U.S. market. The administration is expected to reject those requests, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by Reuters.

What It Means for Global Trade

China's Embassy in Washington criticized the investigation, urging the U.S. to "stop the Section 232 tariff measures as soon as possible, and properly resolve the concerns of all parties through equal dialogue." For Indian-American investors and technology professionals, the action underscores the deepening U.S.-China competition over critical supply chains — and the growing costs of industrial policy that touches everything from rooftop solar to the chips powering AI models.
